source.title: Explaining How Visual, Textual and Multimodal Encoders Share Concepts
source.authors: Clément Cornet; Romaric Besançon; H. Le Borgne

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures cross-model representation similarity with a different method: correlations between sparse-autoencoder features, aggregated as wMPPC. It also compares model sizes, layers, and input datasets.
record.gate_note: The main results are wMPPC scores between encoders, with results separated by source and target modality, dataset, model size, and whether all layers or only the last layer are used. Tables 6–21 provide detailed pairwise scores; the rows below use the corresponding modality aggregates from Table 3. The qualitative feature typologies and the shuffled-feature control are also included. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study compares 20 transformer encoders (vision, text, VLM) using SAE-feature correlations (wMPPC), not the original kernel-alignment method. It varies model size (B vs L), dataset and layer choice, and identifies features shared across model groups. Its own results bear on V1, V2, V5, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add two points. First, the authors find B and L encoders give very similar (B slightly higher) wMPPC, leading to the same conclusions. Second, cross-modal sharing is low even between a VLM's own two encoders. The text-pretraining point is framed as a hypothesis supported by the feature typologies.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK SAEs on encoder activations and compares features using weighted maximum pairwise Pearson correlations and Comparative Sharedness. This differs from directly comparing distances induced by model embeddings.
record.method_sensitivity: wMPPC changes with dataset and layer selection. The study reports that cross-modal comparisons using only the last layer can differ substantially by dataset; all-layer and last-layer averages also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: wMPPC is asymmetric: SigLIP2 text as source to image encoders scores about 0.05, but about 0.17 as target.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Concept sharing between models is directional: one model can contain concepts that another lacks.

fits_no_version.finding: Two SAEs trained on the same CLIP encoder reach wMPPC 0.585, versus 0.0125 when activations are shuffled.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features are reproducible across SAE seeds on a fixed model.

record.problems: The main wMPPC tables report no uncertainty estimates. The authors note that wMPPC is asymmetric and that SAEs are not guaranteed to extract every concept. The study uses encoder models and transformer-based architectures; it does not measure model capability or establish a causal effect of training data or objectives.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed pairwise model results in Tables 6–21 are not individually extracted; the modality-aggregated results in Table 3 are retained, along with the separately reported feature-level findings. The remaining pairwise matrix entries exceed the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Capability is not measured. Size is only B vs L, two points, with no scaling trajectory.
There is no performance measure of the models. Size is used as a proxy only.
Networks trained from different initializations are not compared; only SAE seeds are.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No alternative similarity measures, no neighbour settings, no explicit out-of-distribution test.
No plateau test. No causal isolation of training data.

missing.what: Layer-choice dependence: from all layers to the last layer, same-modality wMPPC roughly halves (I→I 0.463→0.265) while cross-modal stays stable (0.204→0.213). Also the layerwise CLIP heatmap.
SigLIP2's own image and text encoders score 0.050/0.171, below BERT–DinoV2 at 0.177/0.233, despite SigLIP2's state-of-the-art performance.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The size comparison has two sizes only and no uncertainty, so the V1/V2 challenges are weak. All models are transformers, and alignment is measured through SAE features, a different method from mutual-kNN.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares base and large encoders on COCO, but does not measure model capability or show that size and capability increase together. It does not systematically vary architectures, objectives, and training data as a scaling trajectory.
Cross-modal representation similarity is measured, but the study does not test whether alignment rises as both vision and language models improve.
The different-seed comparison is between SAEs trained on the same CLIP encoder, not networks trained from different initializations.
The study does not test mapping one model’s representations onto another’s, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
The study identifies recurring SAE features qualitatively, but does not test whether the same neurons or circuits recur.
The study compares datasets and layer choices, but not alternative similarity measures, neighbourhood settings, or out-of-distribution inputs.
It reports incomplete cross-modal similarity and proposes text pretraining as an explanation, but does not causally isolate shared training data or objectives, or test a plateau.
